title: Unconventional linear transverse exciton transport in valley-layer coupling two-dimensional materials
abstract: Valley-layer coupling (VLC) two-dimensional (2D) materials define a distinct class of quantum systems in which valleys are related by crystal, rather than time-reversal ($\mathcal{T}$) symmetry, enabling gate-controlled valley-contrasted layer polarization. Here we extend this concept to excitons. Using TiSiCo as a prototype VLC material, we show that a perpendicular electric field $E_{\perp}$ controls exciton- dispersion anisotropy and thereby generates unconventional linear transverse exciton transport in both monolayer and twisted bilayer structures. In the monolayer, this response is characterized by anisotropy-induced transverse conductivities, arising from the antisymmetric combination of diagonal elements in the conductivity tensor and strongly tunable by $E_{\perp}$. In the twisted bilayer, symmetry additionally permits transverse responses from the symmetric part of the conductivity tensor. Since intralayer excitons in different layers are connected by the Förster coupling, these symmetric and antisymmetric responses coexist and compete with the recently proposed $\mathcal{T}$-even layer Hall and Nernst exciton counterflow. This interplay is highly tunable by twisted angle, temperature, and the direction of the in-plane driving force, providing a route to disentangle distinct transverse exciton transport signals experimentally. Our results establish $E_{\perp}$ as a powerful knob for controlling exciton transport via VLC and identify VLC 2D materials as a promising platform for engineered excitonic phenomena.
summary: This theoretical work explores unconventional linear transverse exciton transport in valley-layer coupled 2D materials. By using an out-of-plane electric field ($E_{\perp}$), the authors demonstrate control over exciton dispersion anisotropy, which generates measurable transverse currents. This provides a versatile platform for engineering excitonic phenomena in next-generation quantum materials.
main_problem: The paper investigates unconventional linear transverse exciton transport (LTET) in valley-layer coupling (VLC) two-dimensional (2D) materials.
main_result: The perpendicular electric field ($E_{\perp}$) acts as a powerful knob to control exciton-dispersion anisotropy, thereby inducing and tuning LTET in both monolayer and twisted bilayer structures.
method: Theoretical analysis using effective exciton Hamiltonians and semi-classical transport theory to calculate conductivity tensor components.
model_or_system: The system is VLC 2D materials, prototyped by TiSiCo, which exhibit valley coupling via crystal symmetry. The model extends to both monolayer and twisted bilayer configurations, incorporating interlayer Förster coupling.
key_observables: Transverse conductivities ($\sigma_{AS}^{	ext{tra}}, \alpha_{AS}^{	ext{tra}}$) and the competition between anisotropy-induced responses and $\mathcal{T}$-even layer Hall/Nernst counterflow.
important_parameters: Perpendicular electric field ($E_{\perp}$), twist angle ($	heta$), and temperature ($T$).
main_assumptions: The analysis focuses on the zero-Berry-curvature limit and assumes the exciton binding energy is omitted for simplicity.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the crystal structure, exciton dispersion dependence on $E_{\perp}$, and the calculated dependence of transverse conductivities on temperature, $E_{\perp}$, and twist angle for both monolayer and bilayer systems.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical framework for LTET in VLC materials, first analyzing the monolayer response governed by anisotropy, and then extending the analysis to the twisted bilayer where multiple competing transport channels (anisotropy-driven vs. layer counterflow) coexist and are tunable.
why_interesting: The ability to use an external electric field ($E_{\perp}$) to engineer and control specific, symmetry-protected transport channels (like anisotropy-induced currents) in excitonic systems is highly relevant for designing quantum light sources or detectors.
